If there's a moment in Apple technology where the rational and the emotional collide, it's at yesterday's new iPhone launch event.

After watching the iPhone Duo segment of yesterday's keynote this morning, I've already wiped the drool off my desk, but for me, the real stars of yesterday's event were the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max, all thanks to their new camera features……

Variable aperture — with caveats

Given the supply chain required to introduce a variable aperture lens to the iPhone, it's hardly surprising that this feature was leaked extensively before the launch. The only thing that wasn't entirely clear was whether this feature would be available on both Pro models, or only on the Pro Max — the good news is it's the former, with both models getting it.

Apple also confirmed that while the iPhone will automatically adjust the aperture in certain situations, users will also have full manual control. As I mentioned in advance, we may need to temper our expectations on just how much difference this feature will make.

However, I also speculated that Apple may have enhanced Portrait mode capabilities in this latest model, effectively combining a wider aperture with computational photography to achieve better results than hardware alone could deliver. This remains to be verified, but based on some of the sample photos shown, I do suspect I may be right.

I'll be testing this myself, and of course I'll share the results afterwards.

Low-light photography and low-light video

The maximum aperture has also been improved by nearly a full stop — from f/1.78 on the iPhone 17 Pro to f/1.48. While this may not make a huge difference to depth of field itself, it should be a fairly welcome improvement for shooting in low-light conditions (including night scenes).

Manual shutter speed control

In addition to manual aperture control, we can also select shutter speed for both photos and video.

For still photos, this means we can take long exposure shots. The promotional video demonstrated using this feature to create motion blur effects. We don't yet know how long the maximum exposure time can be, nor whether combining the smallest aperture with computational processing can achieve 30-second exposures — a duration typically used to render flowing water with a silky-smooth effect. The same technique can also be used to "erase" passers-by from the frame.

With a traditional camera, achieving this effect would require a neutral density filter (ND filter) to reduce incoming light, but there are third-party iPhone apps that can composite a series of photos into a single image to achieve a similar result. I personally do this often using the Spectre app.

For video, manual shutter speed control allows us to apply the 180-degree rule. When shooting at 24 frames per second, we need to set the shutter speed to 1/48 of a second to achieve the most natural motion blur. This was already possible in third-party professional camera apps like Blackmagic Cam, so it's great to see Apple's built-in camera now capable of the same.

White balance control

Another feature previously only available in third-party apps is white balance control, which has now been added to the built-in camera app.

For still photography, this feature allows us to adjust colour temperature according to our preferences, but it's even more important for video. Automatic white balance means colour temperature — and therefore the overall feel of the image — can shift within a single clip, making things look very amateurish. Being able to lock white balance throughout a clip is a significant improvement.

Cinematic mode for all video

Cinematic mode is essentially the video version of Portrait mode, allowing us to apply an artificial shallow depth of field effect. Until now, we've had to choose between standard video and Cinematic mode video — though the latter still provides us with a "flat" file. The iPhone 18 Pro allows us to decide after shooting standard video whether to apply Cinematic mode effects.

Additionally, we can now shoot in Cinematic mode at frame rates up to 60 frames per second, making it suitable for slow-motion footage.

Intelligent focus mode for video

Existing iPhones already allow you to set focus to track a specific person in the frame, but the iPhone 18 Pro introduces a more advanced version.

It appears to use AI specifically to recognise particular subjects, allowing it to maintain stable tracking even when someone walks between the camera and the subject. Furthermore, even if the subject leaves the frame and re-enters, it can re-acquire the lock.

Histogram

This feature had been rumoured well before yesterday's keynote, so I'll simply recap what I said before.

Battery life

Shooting video consumes a lot of power, so improvements in this area are welcome. We don't have the specifics for video, but given that the Pro Max's maximum battery life has increased from 39 hours to 45 hours, we can expect roughly 15% more shooting time compared to last year's model.

Apple-certified reference images

Finally, there's a way to authenticate a photo when needed. This is clearly a professional tool, primarily relevant to news photographers, law enforcement, and similar roles.

Summary

Of course, some people may only have eyes for the iPhone Duo, which is entirely understandable. But if your iPhone is a significant part of your camera kit, then the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are the real winners this time.
